title.zh: 上采样与转置卷积超详细入门：插值、尺寸公式、棋盘格与 U-Net 解码器
title.en: Upsampling and Transposed Convolution in Depth: Interpolation, Output Size, Checkerboards and U-Net Decoders

description.zh: 从像素网格手算最近邻与双线性插值，拆解转置卷积的散射相加、完整输出尺寸公式和 output_padding，图解棋盘格伪影，并给出 U-Net 解码器的选型与尺寸排错方法。
description.en: Calculate nearest-neighbour and bilinear interpolation on pixel grids, understand scatter-add transposed convolution, the complete output-size formula and output_padding, see why checkerboard artifacts occur, and debug U-Net decoder shapes.

text.zh: 阅读约 26 分钟 · 建议先看网格图，再读公式 图像分类最终只要输出一个类别，特征图可以一路从 $224 \times 224$ 缩到 $7 \times 7$。但语义分割要为每个像素判断类别，输出掩膜通常必须回到接近输入图像的分辨率。 这就需要上采样（upsampling）：把小特征图变成大特征图。 先记住本文最重要的边界： 上采样可以恢复尺寸，但不能凭空找回下采样时已经丢失的信息。它只能依据现有特征进行复制、插值或学习一种合理的填充方式。 在 U-Net 中，跳跃连接把编码器的高分辨率特征送到解码器，正是为了补充单靠上采样无法恢复的边界和位置细节。 阅读前：尺寸、数值和语义是三件不同的事 假设一张 $4 \times 4$ 图经过池化变成 $2 \times 2$： 图中的两张高分辨率图可以下采样成同一个低分辨率结果。只看这个低分辨率结果，无法唯一判断原来是哪一张。这叫信息不可逆。 所以评价一种上采样方法时要分开问： 它能不能得到所需的高和宽？ 它怎样给新增位置赋值？ 它有没有可学习参数？ 它会不会引入规律性的伪影？ 一、先认识四类常见方法 方法 怎样放大 有无参数 常见优点 常见风险 最近邻插值 复制最近的值 无 快、边界值不被平均 块状、锯齿 双线性插值 按距离加权平均 无 平滑、稳定 可能模糊细边界 转置卷积 用可学习核把输入散射到输出 有 放大方式可学习 重叠不均会产生棋盘格 插值 + 卷积 先固定放大，再学习修正 卷积有 职责清楚、通常稳健 有额外计算，仍可能过平滑 此外还有 MaxUnpooling、PixelShuffle、内容感知上采样等，后文会介绍它们适合什么场景。 二、最近邻插值：把一个格子复制成一片 假设输入是一个 $2 \times 2$ 网格： 最近邻放大 2 倍，会把每个值复制成 $2 \times 2$ 小块： 优点： 计算非常快； 不会创造输入中没有的新数值； 对离散标签图，通常比线性插值合理。 缺点： 放大图有明显方块感； 斜线和曲线边缘容易呈阶梯状。 为什么标签掩膜常用最近邻 假设类别标签只有 0 和 1。如果用双线性插值，边界附近可能产生 $0.3$、$0.6$ 等值，它们不是合法类别编号。 如果掩膜是 one-hot 概率或软标签，要根据语义决定；这里说的是整数类别索引图。 三、双线性插值：先横向插，再纵向插 “双线性”可以拆成两次一维线性插值。 先看一维。已知两端： 若某个新位置距离左端占 25%，其值为： $$10 \times 0.75 + 20 \times 0.25 = 12.5$$ 二维位置周围有四个邻居，双线性插值会根据横向、纵向距离对四个值加权。离哪个角近，哪个角权重就大。 一个中心点例子 输入四角为： 几何中心离四个角一样远，因此四个权重都是 $1/4$： $$\frac{0 + 10 + 20 + 30}{4} = 15$$ 真实框架需要根据输入和输出像素中心坐标确定权重，边界处也有明确规则，但“按距离对四邻域加权”是核心直觉。 align_corners 为什么总让人困惑 在 PyTorch 的双线性插值里： align_corners=True：对齐输入与输出最角落像素的中心点；插值坐标会依赖输入和输出尺寸。 align_corners=False：按像素方格的边界对齐，超出部分使用边缘值；对相同 scale_factor 更具尺度一致性，也是多数现代图像任务的默认选择。 这不是“哪个绝对更准确”。如果要复现某篇论文、旧模型或标注处理流程，必须与其设置一致。模型训练和推理时也必须一致。 插值为什么没有可学习参数 权重只由几何距离决定，不通过数据训练。无论处理猫、CT 还是特征图，同样位置关系都会使用同样的插值规则。 这使它稳定、便宜，但也意味着它不知道“器官边界应该更锐利”或“这个纹理应该怎样恢复”。因此常在插值后再接卷积。 四、转置卷积不是卷积的逆运算 它的英文是 transposed convolution，也常被历史代码称为 deconvolution。这个旧称很容易让人误以为它能撤销卷积。 正确理解是：转置的是卷积对应的线性矩阵，不是求逆矩阵。 1. 把普通卷积想成矩阵乘法 把输入摊平成向量 $x$，一次线性卷积可写成： $$y = C x$$ $C$ 是由卷积核和连接方式组成的稀疏矩阵。转置卷积使用同一连接关系的转置： $$z = C^{\mathsf{T}} y$$ 矩阵转置 $C^{\mathsf{T}}$ 一般不等于逆矩阵 $C^{-1}$。所以： 它能把张量映射回较大形状，但数值不会自动复原。 2. “滑动收集”与“散射相加” 理解普通卷积时，我们常想象卷积核在输入上滑动，每次收集一个局部窗口，计算一个输出值。 理解转置卷积时，可以反过来想： 取输入中的一个值； 让它乘以整个卷积核； 把所得小块撒到输出对应区域； 多个小块重叠的位置做加法。 这个“散射并相加”的视角，比“它是一种反卷积”更准确，也直接解释了棋盘格伪影为什么与重叠次数有关。 3. 等价的插零视角 对常见配置，转置卷积也可看成： 在相邻输入元素之间插入 $s - 1$ 个零； 按参数决定边界扩展或裁剪； 用步幅 1 做一次普通卷积式计算。 图中使用 kernel=2, stride=2, padding=0：$2 \times 2$ 输入经过等价过程得到 $4 \times 4$ 输出。插入的零只是帮助理解计算连接，不代表网络最终会在输出中留下零。 4. 一个最简单的数值例子 输入： 卷积核全为 1，kernel=2, stride=2, padding=0。因为核大小刚好等于步幅，各输入展开的小块互不重叠： 这里结果恰好像最近邻复制，是因为卷积核特意设成了全 1。真实训练中核权重会学习，四个位置不必相等。 五、转置卷积输出尺寸公式 先写一维公式，高和宽分别计算。完整形式是： $$H_{\text{out}} = (H_{\text{in}} - 1)\ s - 2p + d\ (k - 1) + p_{\text{out}} + 1$$ 当 $d = 1$ 时，可化简为常见版本： $$H_{\text{out}} = (H_{\text{in}} - 1)\ s - 2p + k + p_{\text{out}}$$ 每个参数的直觉 参数 符号 代码参数 作用 输入尺寸 $H_{\text{in}}$ — 当前特征图高或宽 步幅 $s$ stride 相邻输入值在输出中的展开起点相隔多远 卷积核 $k$ kernel_size 每个输入值影响多大范围 padding $p$ padding 在转置尺寸关系中抵消两侧范围，数值越大输出越小 dilation $d$ dilation 拉开核元素间隔 output padding $p_{\text{out}}$ output_padding 在多种可行输出尺寸中选择其中一个 例 1：最常见的 2 倍放大 取 $H_{\text{in}} = 16$、$s = 2$、$k = 2$、$p = 0$、$p_{\text{out}} = 0$： $$H_{\text{out}} = (16 - 1) \times 2 - 0 + 2 = 32$$ 对应代码： 例 2：kernel=4 也能放大 2 倍 取 $H_{\text{in}} = 16$、$s = 2$、$k = 4$、$p = 1$： $$H_{\text{out}} = (16 - 1) \times 2 - 2 + 4 = 32$$ 例 3：为什么需要 output_padding 普通 stride=2 卷积会跳过位置并使用向下取整，因此不同输入尺寸可能得到同一个输出尺寸。反过来只知道小特征图时，大尺寸不一定唯一。 例如： 取 $H_{\text{in}} = 5$、$s = 2$、$k = 3$、$p = 1$： $$\begin{aligned}p_{\text{out}} = 0 &\ \Longrightarrow\ H_{\text{out}} = 9 \crp_{\text{out}} = 1 &\ \Longrightarrow\ H_{\text{out}} = 10\end{aligned}$$ $p_{\text{out}}$（代码里的 output_padding）用来选 9 还是 10。它主要调整输出形状，不是在已经算好的输出四周真的补一圈零，也不会因此新增可学习参数。 为什么转置卷积里的 padding 很反直觉 普通卷积公式里，给输入补边通常让输出更大；转置卷积公式里出现 $-2p$，参数越大输出反而越小。 一个实用策略是：不要只凭“padding”这个名字猜，直接把参数代入公式，并用一个随机张量在框架中打印 shape 验证。 六、棋盘格伪影是怎么产生的 转置卷积最著名的问题是输出出现周期性的明暗格或网格纹理，叫棋盘格伪影（checkerboard artifacts）。 1. 一维先看懂覆盖次数 假设 $k = 3$、$s = 2$。每个输入值影响连续 3 个输出位置，但下一个输入的展开起点向右移动 2 格： 中间区域会交替出现“被覆盖 2 次”和“被覆盖 1 次”的位置。即使输入和权重差不多，被加两次的位置也天然更容易数值偏大。 二维中，横向和纵向的不均匀叠加，形成棋盘格： 2. 为什么 kernel 能被 stride 整除更安全 常见安全起点： 它们更容易形成均匀覆盖。危险例子： 但“可以整除”只是消除了结构上的一类不均匀，并不保证模型绝不会学出周期纹理。损失函数、初始化、边界处理和后续卷积都可能影响最终伪影。 3. 怎样判断伪影来自上采样 观察预测图或生成图： 纹理是否以固定像素周期重复； 横向和纵向是否形成规则格子； 将转置卷积换成插值 + 卷积后，格子是否明显减弱； 模型刚初始化、还未充分训练时是否已有周期图案。 规则而全局一致的网格更像结构伪影；只出现在真实边界附近的错误可能是特征不足、标签噪声或损失设计问题，不能都怪转置卷积。 七、插值 + 卷积：把“放大”和“学习”拆开 一种常见做法是： 职责非常清楚： 它避免了转置卷积因“散射区域重叠次数不均”产生的典型棋盘格机制。不过任何可学习网络都仍可能产生其他纹理伪影，不能把它理解成数学上保证“绝无伪影”。 最近邻 + 卷积还是双线性 + 卷积 最近邻 + 卷积： 先复制，不主动平滑；卷积再学习怎样融合。生成模型和一些解码器常用。 双线性 + 卷积： 起点更平滑；分割中常用，但极细边界可能被软化。 没有对所有数据都最优的固定答案。边界敏感任务可以同时比较 Dice、Hausdorff distance 和可视化，而不是只看平均损失。 与转置卷积公平比较参数量 不能只说哪一个“有参数”。两者通常都有可学习权重： $$\begin{aligned}\text{ConvTranspose} &: k \times k \times C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}} \cr\text{Upsample} + \text{Conv} &: 3 \times 3 \times C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}\end{aligned}$$ 插值本身无参数，但后面的卷积有。若转置卷积用 $k = 2$，它甚至可能比一个 $3 \times 3$ 卷积参数少。速度和显存也依赖具体形状、实现和硬件，需要实测。 八、U-Net 解码器里到底发生了什么 典型 U-Net 解码块不是只有上采样，而是四步： 深层特征上采样； 与编码器同尺度特征对齐； 沿通道维拼接； 用卷积融合两路信息。 例如： 拼接用的是： 这里是通道拼接，不是 ResNet 的逐元素相加。拼接允许两路通道完整保留，但也会让后续卷积输入通道数相加。 一个完整的上采样块 示例中为讲清逻辑，self.up 后又做了必要时的尺寸对齐。真实工程也可直接在 forward 中一次性插值到 skip.shape[-2:]，避免重复计算。 九、奇数尺寸为什么经常差一个像素 假设输入高为 321，stride=2 下采样时会涉及向下取整或 padding： 再简单乘 2，可能得到 320 或 322，不一定回到 321。经过多级下采样后，每一级的舍入都会影响对应跳跃连接。 常用解决办法有三种： 方法 1：直接插值到 skip 的尺寸 这是最直接、可读性很高的办法。 方法 2：对称 padding 只适合 x 比 skip 小；如果差值可能为负，还要考虑裁剪。 方法 3：训练前把输入 pad 到网络步长的倍数 若编码器总下采样 5 次，总步长通常是 $2^5 = 32$。可以先把高宽 pad 到 32 的倍数，预测后再裁回原尺寸。滑窗推理和医学影像框架常采用这种思路。 十、另外三种上采样方式 1. MaxUnpooling：把最大值放回原位置 MaxPool 不只可以输出最大值，还可以记录最大值来自窗口中的哪个位置。MaxUnpooling 利用这些索引： 空位置仍是 0，需要后续卷积填充。SegNet 采用这种方法。它保存位置索引，但不能恢复被最大池化丢掉的其他数值。 2. PixelShuffle：把通道搬到空间 放大倍数为 $r$ 时，先用卷积生成 $C_{\text{out}} \cdot r^2$ 个通道，再重排： $$(N,\ C_{\text{out}} r^2,\ H,\ W) \ \xrightarrow{\ \text{PixelShuffle}(r)\ } \ (N,\ C_{\text{out}},\ Hr,\ Wr)$$ 它在超分辨率中很常见。它没有转置卷积的重叠覆盖机制，但不同子像素通道如果初始化或学习不一致，也可能出现周期纹理，所以不能简单等同于“绝对没有棋盘格”。 3. 内容感知上采样 CARAFE 等方法会根据局部内容预测重组权重，不再使用对所有位置都相同的固定插值规则。它可能更好地保留结构，但实现、计算和部署复杂度也更高，通常不是入门 U-Net 的第一选择。 十一、到底应该选哪一种 如果你正在写第一个 U-Net 先使用： 理由不是它在所有任务上都最准，而是行为清楚、尺寸容易控制、典型棋盘格风险较低，适合作为可靠基线。 如果论文或官方实现指定转置卷积 忠实复现，并检查： kernel_size 是否能被 stride 整除； padding 与 output_padding 是否给出目标尺寸； 奇数输入时各级 shape 是否与 skip 对齐； 输出可视化中是否出现周期网格。 经典 U-Net 和许多 nnU-Net 配置都可以合理地使用转置卷积。不能因为存在棋盘格风险，就断言所有转置卷积都不好。 如果处理离散标签掩膜 通常使用最近邻，避免制造不存在的类别编号。模型 logits 或连续概率图则可以按任务使用双线性插值。 如果做超分辨率 PixelShuffle、resize-convolution 和专门设计的重建模块都值得比较；评价重点不仅是像素误差，还包括纹理真实性和周期伪影。 一个简短决策表 需求 建议起点 最容易实现和排错的分割解码器 双线性插值 + 3×3 卷积 严格复现经典 U-Net / 指定架构 按原配置使用转置卷积 离散类别 mask 缩放 最近邻 超分辨率 PixelShuffle 或专门重建模块 要利用池化位置索引 MaxUnpooling 边界极敏感 比较多种上采样，并保留高分辨率 skip 十二、初学者最容易犯的十个错误 错误 1：认为上采样能找回原始细节 它只能扩大现有表示；丢失信息要依靠跳跃连接、上下文和学习到的先验补偿。 错误 2：把转置卷积叫作卷积的逆 它对应卷积线性算子的转置，不是逆运算。 错误 3：把 output_padding 当成真正补零 它用于消除输出形状歧义，主要选择输出尺寸，不是在输出图周围附加一圈实际零值。 错误 4：只看 scale factor，不打印 shape 奇数输入、多层 stride、padding 和 dilation 会共同影响尺寸。调试时直接打印每一级 x.shape 和 skip.shape。 错误 5：用双线性插值缩放整数类别 mask 这会制造无效类别值。整数标签一般使用最近邻。 错误 6：训练和推理使用不同的 align_corners 坐标映射变化会导致输出错位，尤其影响边界。 错误 7：认为 kernel 能被 stride 整除就绝无棋盘格 它只解决不均匀覆盖这一主要结构原因，模型仍可能学习到周期模式。 错误 8：上采样后直接与 skip 相加 标准 U-Net 通常按通道拼接；若要相加，两路通道数和语义都需专门设计。 错误 9：拼接后忘记通道数相加 $128$ 通道上采样特征与 $128$ 通道 skip 拼接后是 $256$ 通道，后续卷积的 in_channels 必须写 256。 错误 10：只比较参数量，不比较计算位置 在高分辨率特征图上做 3×3 卷积可能很贵。上采样前后何时降通道，会明显影响 FLOPs 和显存。 十三、用最小实验验证尺寸 遇到公式不确定时，不要靠猜： 手算高度和宽度： $$\begin{aligned}H_{\text{out}} &= (5 - 1) \times 2 - 2 \times 1 + 3 + 1 = 10 \crW_{\text{out}} &= (7 - 1) \times 2 - 2 \times 1 + 3 + 1 = 14\end{aligned}$$ 把公式、代码输出和网络目标尺寸三者对上，尺寸问题通常就解决了。 十四、四道自测题 1. 最近邻把 2×2 放大两倍时，每个输入值会变成多少个输出值？在二维中会复制成 $2 \times 2$ 区域，因此每个输入值对应 4 个输出位置。 2. ConvTranspose2d 的 in=8、kernel=4、stride=2、padding=1、output_padding=0，输出多大？$(8-1) \times 2 - 2 \times 1 + 4 = 16$，所以该维度正好放大两倍。 3. 为什么 kernel=3、stride=2 更容易出现棋盘格？因为每个输入展开到 3 个位置，而起点每次移动 2 格，内部输出位置会交替被覆盖 1 次和 2 次；二维叠加后形成网格状不均匀。 4. U-Net 上采样后是 128×64×64，skip 也是 128×64×64，按通道拼接后 shape 是什么？忽略 batch 维时是 $256 \times 64 \times 64$。空间尺寸不变，通道数相加。 最后用一张清单复习 上采样恢复的是网格尺寸，不保证恢复丢失信息。 最近邻复制值；双线性按四周距离加权；二者都没有学习参数。 离散类别 mask 通常使用最近邻，不要插出小数类别。 转置卷积是矩阵转置意义上的卷积，不是逆卷积。 理解转置卷积可以用“每个输入把加权小块散射到输出，再把重叠相加”。 完整输出公式要考虑 stride、padding、kernel、dilation 和 output_padding。 output_padding 用于选择输出形状，不是给最终结果真的补零。 棋盘格的主要结构原因是重叠覆盖不均匀。 kernel 能被 stride 整除是更安全的起点，但不是无伪影保证。 U-Net 通常先上采样，再与 skip 按通道拼接，最后卷积融合。 输入为奇数尺寸时，直接对齐到 skip.shape[-2:] 往往最容易排错。 参考资料 Dumoulin & Visin, A Guide to Convolution Arithmetic for Deep Learning, arXiv:1603.07285 Odena et al., Deconvolution and Checkerboard Artifacts, Distill 2016, distill.pub/2016/deconv-checkerboard Ronneberger et al., U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation, arXiv:1505.04597 Badrinarayanan et al., SegNet, TPAMI 2017, arXiv:1511.00561 Shi et al., Real-Time Single Image and Video Super-Resolution with an Efficient Sub-Pixel CNN, CVPR 2016, arXiv:1609.05158 PyTorch, ConvTranspose2d 文档
text.en: About 26 minutes · Read the grid diagrams before the formulas Image classification only needs to output one class, so its feature maps can shrink all the way from $224\times224$ to $7\times7$. Semantic segmentation must classify every pixel, so the output mask normally needs to return to almost the input image’s resolution. This requires upsampling: turning a small feature map into a larger one. First remember the most important boundary in this article: Upsampling can restore spatial size, but it cannot magically recover information that was discarded during downsampling. It can only copy, interpolate or learn a plausible way to fill new positions from the remaining features. In U-Net, skip connections deliver high-resolution encoder features to the decoder precisely because upsampling alone cannot reconstruct all boundary and positional detail. Before reading: size, values and semantics are different things Suppose pooling reduces a $4\times4$ image to $2\times2$: The two high-resolution patterns in the diagram can produce the same low-resolution output. Looking only at that output, we cannot know which original was present. This is irreversible information loss. When evaluating an upsampling method, ask four separate questions: Can it produce the required height and width? How does it assign values to new positions? Does it have learnable parameters? Can it introduce regular artifacts? 1. Four common families of methods Method How it enlarges Parameters? Common advantage Common risk Nearest-neighbour interpolation copies the nearest value no fast; does not average boundary labels blockiness and stair-step edges Bilinear interpolation distance-weighted average no smooth and stable may blur fine boundaries Transposed convolution uses a learned kernel to scatter inputs into the output yes learns how to enlarge uneven overlap can produce checkerboards Interpolation + convolution fixed enlargement, then learned correction convolution only clear responsibilities and usually robust extra computation and possible oversmoothing MaxUnpooling, PixelShuffle and content-aware upsampling are also useful. Later sections explain when to consider them. 2. Nearest-neighbour interpolation: copy one cell into a region Suppose the input is a $2\times2$ grid: Nearest-neighbour upsampling by a factor of two copies each value into a $2\times2$ block: Advantages: extremely fast; creates no new numerical values that were absent from the input; usually sensible for discrete label maps. Disadvantages: the enlarged image looks blocky; diagonal and curved boundaries become staircase-shaped. Why do label masks normally use nearest neighbour? Suppose class labels can only be 0 or 1. Bilinear interpolation can produce 0.3 or 0.6 near a boundary, and those are not valid class indices. One-hot probabilities and soft labels require a decision based on their semantics. The rule above applies to integer class-index maps. 3. Bilinear interpolation: interpolate horizontally, then vertically “Bilinear” can be understood as two one-dimensional linear interpolations. First consider one dimension: If a new position is 25% of the way from the left endpoint, its value is: $$10\times0.75+20\times0.25=12.5$$ A two-dimensional position has four neighbours. Bilinear interpolation weights them according to horizontal and vertical distance: the closer a corner, the larger its weight. A centre-point example Suppose the four input corners are: The geometric centre is equally far from all four corners, so every weight is $1/4$: $$\frac{0+10+20+30}{4}=15$$ Real frameworks determine weights from the centres of input and output pixels and define precise boundary behaviour. “Weight the four neighbours by distance” is the essential intuition. Why is align_corners confusing? In PyTorch bilinear interpolation: align_corners=True aligns the centres of the corner pixels in the input and output; coordinates depend on both input and output size. align_corners=False aligns the outer boundaries of the pixel squares and uses edge values outside the range. It is more scale-consistent for the same scale_factor and is the default choice in most modern vision tasks. Neither setting is universally “more accurate”. To reproduce a paper, legacy model or annotation pipeline, use the same setting. Training and inference must also agree. Why does interpolation have no learnable parameters? Weights depend only on geometric distance and are not trained from data. The same spatial relationship uses the same rule whether the input is a cat, a CT scan or a feature map. That makes interpolation stable and cheap, but it cannot know that an organ boundary should be sharper or a texture should be reconstructed in a particular way. A convolution is therefore often applied afterwards. 4. A transposed convolution is not the inverse of a convolution The correct name is transposed convolution, although historical code often calls it “deconvolution”. That old name easily suggests that it can undo a convolution. The accurate statement is: the matrix representing the convolution is transposed; it is not inverted. 4.1 View an ordinary convolution as matrix multiplication Flatten the input into a vector $x$. A linear convolution can be written as: $$y=Cx$$ $C$ is a sparse matrix determined by the kernel and connectivity. A transposed convolution uses the transpose of that connectivity: $$z=C^{\mathsf T}y$$ In general, $C^{\mathsf T}$ is not the inverse $C^{-1}$. Therefore: It can map a tensor back to a larger shape, but its values are not automatically reconstructed. 4.2 “Gather while sliding” versus “scatter and add” We often picture an ordinary convolution sliding a kernel over the input, gathering a local window and producing one output value. For a transposed convolution, reverse the perspective: take one input value; multiply it by the complete kernel; scatter the resulting patch into the corresponding output region; add patches wherever they overlap. This scatter-add view is more accurate than “inverse convolution” and directly explains why checkerboards depend on overlap counts. 4.3 An equivalent zero-insertion view For common settings, a transposed convolution can also be viewed as: insert $s-1$ zeros between adjacent input values; expand or crop the boundary according to the parameters; perform an ordinary stride-1 convolution-style computation. The diagram uses kernel=2, stride=2, padding=0: a $2\times2$ input becomes a $4\times4$ output. Inserted zeros are only a way to understand connectivity; they do not mean the trained network must leave zeros in the final output. 4.4 The simplest numerical example Input: Let every kernel value be 1 and use kernel=2, stride=2, padding=0. Kernel size equals stride, so the patches produced by different inputs do not overlap: This happens to look like nearest-neighbour copying only because the kernel was deliberately filled with ones. During real training the weights are learned and the four positions need not be equal. 5. Output-size formula for transposed convolution Write the one-dimensional formula first and apply it separately to height and width: $$H_{\text{out}}=(H_{\text{in}}-1)s-2p+d(k-1)+p_{\text{out}}+1$$ When $d=1$, it simplifies to the familiar form: $$H_{\text{out}}=(H_{\text{in}}-1)s-2p+k+p_{\text{out}}$$ Intuition for every parameter Parameter Symbol Code argument Role Input size $H_{\text{in}}$ — current feature-map height or width Stride $s$ stride distance between the output starting points of adjacent input values Kernel $k$ kernel_size region influenced by one input value Padding $p$ padding cancels extent on both sides; larger values reduce the transposed-convolution output Dilation $d$ dilation spreads kernel elements apart Output padding $p_{\text{out}}$ output_padding selects one of several possible output sizes Example 1: the most common 2× enlargement Take $H_{\text{in}}=16$, $s=2$, $k=2$, $p=0$ and $p_{\text{out}}=0$: $$H_{\text{out}}=(16-1)\times2-0+2=32$$ Example 2: kernel=4 can also enlarge by two Take $H_{\text{in}}=16$, $s=2$, $k=4$ and $p=1$: $$H_{\text{out}}=(16-1)\times2-2+4=32$$ Example 3: why is output_padding needed? An ordinary stride-2 convolution skips positions and rounds down, so different input sizes can produce the same output size. In the reverse direction, knowing only the small feature map does not uniquely determine the larger size. For $H_{\text{in}}=5$, $s=2$, $k=3$ and $p=1$: $$\begin{aligned}p_{\text{out}}=0 &\ \Longrightarrow\ H_{\text{out}}=9 \crp_{\text{out}}=1 &\ \Longrightarrow\ H_{\text{out}}=10\end{aligned}$$ output_padding selects 9 or 10. It mainly resolves the output shape. It does not literally append a ring of zeros around an already computed output, and it adds no learnable parameters. Why does transposed-convolution padding feel backwards? In the ordinary-convolution formula, padding the input normally makes the output larger. The transposed-convolution formula contains $-2p$, so increasing padding makes its output smaller. A practical rule is not to guess from the word “padding”. Substitute the values into the formula and verify the result by printing the shape of a random tensor in the framework. 6. Where do checkerboard artifacts come from? The best-known transposed-convolution problem is a periodic bright-and-dark grid called a checkerboard artifact. 6.1 Understand overlap counts in one dimension Let $k=3$ and $s=2$. Each input affects three consecutive output positions, but the next patch starts two positions later: The interior alternates between positions covered twice and once. Even when inputs and weights are similar, values receiving two additions are naturally more likely to be larger. In two dimensions, horizontal and vertical unevenness multiply into a checkerboard: 6.2 Why is kernel divisible by stride a safer starting point? Common safer configurations are: They more readily produce even coverage. Riskier examples are: Divisibility only removes one structural source of unevenness. It does not guarantee that a model can never learn periodic texture. Losses, initialisation, boundary handling and later convolutions all affect the final artifacts. 6.3 How can you tell whether an artifact comes from upsampling? Inspect the prediction or generated image: does the texture repeat at a fixed pixel period? do horizontal and vertical lines form a regular grid? does replacing transposed convolution with interpolation plus convolution greatly reduce the pattern? is a periodic pattern visible immediately after initialisation, before substantial training? A regular global grid suggests a structural artifact. Errors restricted to real object boundaries may instead come from weak features, label noise or the loss function; do not blame every boundary error on transposed convolution. 7. Interpolation + convolution: separate enlargement from learning A common block is: Responsibilities are explicit: This avoids the classic checkerboard mechanism caused by unevenly overlapping scatter regions. Any learned network can still produce other texture artifacts, so this is not a mathematical guarantee of artifact-free output. Nearest + convolution or bilinear + convolution? Nearest + convolution: copy first without deliberate smoothing; let the convolution learn how to mix. Common in generative models and some decoders. Bilinear + convolution: starts from a smoother feature map and is common in segmentation, but may soften very thin boundaries. No fixed choice wins on every dataset. For boundary-sensitive tasks, compare Dice, Hausdorff distance and visualisations rather than only the average loss. Compare parameters fairly with transposed convolution It is not enough to ask which method “has parameters”. Both usually contain learned weights: $$\begin{aligned}\text{ConvTranspose}&: k\times k\times C_{\text{in}}\times C_{\text{out}} \cr\text{Upsample} + \text{Conv}&: 3\times3\times C_{\text{in}}\times C_{\text{out}}\end{aligned}$$ Interpolation itself has no parameters, but the following convolution does. A transposed convolution with $k=2$ can even have fewer parameters than a 3×3 convolution. Speed and memory also depend on the exact shapes, implementation and hardware, so benchmark them. 8. What actually happens in a U-Net decoder? A typical U-Net decoder block is not just an upsampling operation. It performs four steps: upsample the deep feature map; align it to the encoder feature at the same scale; concatenate them along the channel dimension; use convolutions to fuse the two sources. For example: Concatenation is written as: This is channel concatenation, not the element-wise addition used in ResNet. Concatenation preserves both channel sets but makes the next convolution’s input channel count equal to their sum. A complete upsampling block The example first uses self.up and then performs alignment only when necessary to expose the logic. Production code can interpolate directly to skip.shape[-2:] once inside forward and avoid duplicate work. 9. Why are odd input sizes often off by one pixel? Suppose the input height is 321. A stride-2 downsampling operation rounds according to its padding and formula: Simply multiplying by two later gives 320 or 322, not necessarily 321. After several downsampling stages, rounding at each stage affects the corresponding skip connection. Three common solutions are: Method 1: interpolate directly to the skip size This is the most direct and readable method. Method 2: symmetric padding This only handles the case where x is smaller than skip. If a difference can be negative, cropping must also be considered. Method 3: pad inputs to a multiple of the network stride If an encoder downsamples five times, its total stride is normally $2^5=32$. Pad height and width to multiples of 32 before the network, then crop the prediction back to the original size. Sliding-window inference and medical-imaging frameworks often follow this approach. 10. Three other upsampling methods 10.1 MaxUnpooling: put maxima back at their original positions MaxPool can output not only each maximum value but also the index from which it came. MaxUnpooling uses those indices: Empty positions remain zero and need later convolutions to fill them. SegNet uses this method. It preserves positional indices but cannot recover the other values discarded by max pooling. 10.2 PixelShuffle: move channels into space For enlargement factor $r$, a convolution first produces $C_{\text{out}}r^2$ channels and then rearranges them: $$(N,\ C_{\text{out}}r^2,\ H,\ W)\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{PixelShuffle}(r)\ }\ (N,\ C_{\text{out}},\ Hr,\ Wr)$$ It is common in super-resolution. PixelShuffle lacks the overlapping-patch mechanism of transposed convolution, but inconsistent initialisation or learning between sub-pixel channels can still create periodic texture. It is not automatically “checkerboard-proof”. 10.3 Content-aware upsampling Methods such as CARAFE predict reassembly weights from local content instead of applying the same fixed interpolation rule everywhere. They may preserve structure better, but increase implementation, compute and deployment complexity and are not usually the first choice for a beginner U-Net. 11. Which method should you choose? If you are implementing your first U-Net Start with: Not because it is always the most accurate, but because its behaviour is clear, its sizes are easy to control and its risk of classic checkerboards is low. It is a reliable baseline. If a paper or official implementation specifies transposed convolution Reproduce it faithfully and check: whether kernel_size is divisible by stride; whether padding and output_padding produce the target size; whether odd-sized inputs align at every skip connection; whether output visualisations contain a periodic grid. Classic U-Net and many nnU-Net configurations use transposed convolution successfully. The existence of checkerboard risk does not make every transposed convolution bad. If you are resizing a discrete label mask Normally use nearest neighbour so that no invalid class indices are invented. Model logits and continuous probability maps may use bilinear interpolation when appropriate. If you are working on super-resolution Compare PixelShuffle, resize-convolution and specialised reconstruction modules. Evaluate not only pixel error but also texture realism and periodic artifacts. Short decision table Need Suggested starting point Easiest segmentation decoder to implement and debug bilinear interpolation + 3×3 convolution Exact reproduction of classic U-Net or a specified architecture use the stated transposed convolution Resize a discrete class mask nearest neighbour Super-resolution PixelShuffle or a specialised reconstruction module Reuse pooling-location indices MaxUnpooling Extremely boundary-sensitive task compare several methods and preserve high-resolution skips 12. Ten mistakes beginners often make Mistake 1: assuming upsampling recovers the original detail It only enlarges the remaining representation. Lost information must be compensated by skip connections, contextual features and learned priors. Mistake 2: calling transposed convolution the inverse of convolution It corresponds to the transpose of convolution’s linear operator, not its inverse. Mistake 3: treating output_padding as literal zero-padding It resolves an output-shape ambiguity. It does not append actual zeros around the final output. Mistake 4: checking only the scale factor instead of printing shapes Odd inputs, several strides, padding and dilation all affect the size. Print x.shape and skip.shape at every level while debugging. Mistake 5: resizing an integer class mask with bilinear interpolation This creates invalid class values. Integer labels normally use nearest neighbour. Mistake 6: changing align_corners between training and inference The coordinate mapping changes and can shift the output, especially near boundaries. Mistake 7: believing divisibility guarantees no checkerboards It removes the main structural source of uneven coverage, but the model can still learn periodic patterns. Mistake 8: adding the upsampled feature directly to the skip Standard U-Net concatenates along the channel dimension. Addition requires deliberately matched channel counts and compatible semantics. Mistake 9: forgetting that concatenation adds channel counts Concatenating a 128-channel upsampled feature with a 128-channel skip produces 256 channels. The next convolution must use in_channels=256. Mistake 10: comparing parameter counts but ignoring where computation happens A 3×3 convolution on a high-resolution feature map can be expensive. Whether channels are reduced before or after upsampling can substantially change FLOPs and memory use. 13. Verify sizes with a minimal experiment When uncertain about the formula, do not guess: Calculate height and width by hand: $$\begin{aligned}H_{\text{out}}&=(5-1)\times2-2\times1+3+1=10 \crW_{\text{out}}&=(7-1)\times2-2\times1+3+1=14\end{aligned}$$ Once the formula, code output and intended network size agree, most shape problems are solved. 14. Four self-check questions 1. When nearest neighbour enlarges a 2×2 grid by a factor of twoIn two dimensions it becomes a $2\times2$ region, so every input value corresponds to four output positions. 2. ConvTranspose2d has input size 8$(8-1)\times2-2\times1+4=16$, so that dimension is exactly doubled. 3. Why is kernel=3Each input spreads to three positions while starting points move by two. Interior output positions alternate between one and two overlaps; in two dimensions the unevenness forms a grid. 4. A U-Net upsampled feature is 128×64×64 and the skip is also 128×64×64. What is the shape after channel concatenation?Ignoring the batch dimension, it is $256\times64\times64$. Spatial size is unchanged and channel counts are added. Final review checklist Upsampling restores grid size but does not guarantee recovery of lost information. Nearest neighbour copies values; bilinear interpolation weights four neighbours by distance; neither has learned parameters. Discrete class masks normally use nearest neighbour so interpolation does not invent fractional classes. Transposed convolution is a convolution in the matrix-transpose sense, not an inverse convolution. Understand it as each input scattering a weighted patch into the output and overlapping patches being added. The complete output formula includes stride, padding, kernel, dilation and output padding. output_padding selects the output shape; it does not literally pad the final result with zeros. Uneven overlap is the main structural source of checkerboard artifacts. A kernel divisible by the stride is a safer starting point, not an artifact-free guarantee. U-Net normally upsamples, concatenates with the skip along channels, and then fuses with convolution. For odd input sizes, directly matching skip.shape[-2:] is often the easiest solution to debug. References Dumoulin & Visin, A Guide to Convolution Arithmetic for Deep Learning, arXiv:1603.07285 Odena et al., Deconvolution and Checkerboard Artifacts, Distill 2016, distill.pub/2016/deconv-checkerboard Ronneberger et al., U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation, arXiv:1505.04597 Badrinarayanan et al., SegNet, TPAMI 2017, arXiv:1511.00561 Shi et al., Real-Time Single Image and Video Super-Resolution with an Efficient Sub-Pixel CNN, CVPR 2016, arXiv:1609.05158 PyTorch, ConvTranspose2d documentation

title.en: BatchNorm Explained in Depth: Manual Calculation, Train vs. Eval, and Choosing BN/LN/IN/GN

description.zh: 从四个数字手算 BatchNorm，图解 NCHW 上的统计范围、gamma/beta、running mean/var、train/eval 模式，并比较 LayerNorm、InstanceNorm 与 GroupNorm，解释小 batch 和医学影像中的选择。
description.en: Calculate BatchNorm from four numbers, see exactly which NCHW elements are normalised together, understand gamma/beta, running mean/variance and train/eval behaviour, and compare BatchNorm, LayerNorm, InstanceNorm and GroupNorm for small-batch medical imaging.

text.zh: 阅读约 24 分钟 · 包含手算、代码和排错清单 BatchNorm 常被缩写成 BN。你会在网络代码里反复看到这样的组合： 它看起来像一个无关紧要的“标准配件”，实际上同时影响训练速度、学习率、批大小、验证结果和模型部署。ResNet 中几乎每个卷积后都有 BN；如果不理解它的训练与推理差异，很容易遇到“训练很好、验证突然变差”“同一张图每次预测不一样”之类的问题。 先给出一句最直观的解释： BatchNorm 会在每个通道内，把一批数据拉回到较稳定的数值尺度，再允许模型用可学习参数把它缩放和平移到最合适的位置。 阅读前：什么叫“归一化” 假设两门考试的难度不同： 只看原始分数，95 好像远强于 70；但如果还知道每场考试的均值和分数波动，就能判断“你比同场平均水平高多少”。归一化做的是类似的事：不只看原值，而是看它相对所在分布的位置。 神经网络各层输出的尺度会随参数更新不断改变。某层今天输出大多在 [-1, 1]，训练几步后可能变成 [-20, 20]。后面的层就像不断面对评分标准变化的试卷，优化会更困难。BN 通过动态标准化，帮助数值保持在较可控的范围。 论文名片 论文： Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift 作者： Sergey Ioffe、Christian Szegedy 会议： ICML 2015 论文地址： arXiv:1502.03167 原论文用“减少内部协变量偏移”解释 BN。后续研究发现，这不是完整答案；BN 对优化曲面和梯度的平滑作用可能更关键。本文会把“它怎么算”“代码怎么表现”和“为什么可能有效”分开讲，避免把假说当成公式本身。 一、先用四个数字手算一次 暂时忘掉图片和通道，假设一个小批次里只有四个数： $$x = [\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\ ]$$ 第 1 步：计算均值 $$\mu = \frac{1 + 3 + 5 + 7}{4} = 4$$ 均值表示这一组数据的中心。 第 2 步：计算方差 先看每个数离均值多远，再平方、求平均： $$(1-4)^2 = 9 \qquad (3-4)^2 = 1 \qquad (5-4)^2 = 1 \qquad (7-4)^2 = 9$$ $$\sigma^2 = \frac{9 + 1 + 1 + 9}{4} = 5$$ 方差表示数据分散程度。平方是为了不让正负偏差互相抵消。 第 3 步：标准化 $$\hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}$$ 暂时忽略很小的 $\epsilon$，标准差是 $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$： $$\begin{aligned}1 &\longrightarrow (1-4)/2.236 \approx -1.342 \cr3 &\longrightarrow (3-4)/2.236 \approx -0.447 \cr5 &\longrightarrow (5-4)/2.236 \approx +0.447 \cr7 &\longrightarrow (7-4)/2.236 \approx +1.342\end{aligned}$$ 标准化后的四个数均值约为 0，方差约为 1。 第 4 步：可学习地缩放和平移 BN 不会停在 $\hat{x}$，还会计算： $$y = \gamma \hat{x} + \beta$$ 假设模型学到 $\gamma = 2$、$\beta = 0.5$： $$\begin{aligned}-1.342 &\longrightarrow -2.184 \cr-0.447 &\longrightarrow -0.394 \cr+0.447 &\longrightarrow +1.394 \cr+1.342 &\longrightarrow +3.184\end{aligned}$$ $\gamma$ 和 $\beta$ 不是人工指定的超参数，而是像卷积核一样通过反向传播学习的参数。 为什么标准化之后还要“改回去” 如果所有特征都被强制固定为零均值、单位方差，可能限制网络表达能力。$\gamma$ 和 $\beta$ 给模型选择权： $\gamma$ 控制拉伸或压缩； $\beta$ 控制整体左移或右移。 例如模型若发现原来的分布最合适，可以学习到恰当的 $\gamma$、$\beta$，在给定统计量下恢复所需的尺度与位置。因此 BN 不是简单粗暴地把所有层永久锁死在同一个分布上。 二、图片上的 BN 到底对哪些数字求均值 卷积层输出通常是四维张量： $$(N,\ C,\ H,\ W)$$ 维度 含义 例子 $N$ batch 中的样本数 一次送入 8 张图 $C$ 通道数 64 张特征图 $H$ 特征图高度 56 $W$ 特征图宽度 56 BatchNorm2d(C) 为每一个通道单独计算统计量。对通道 c，它收集： 也就是所有样本在该通道的全部空间位置，共 $N \times H \times W$ 个值。 对每个通道 $c$： $$\mu_c = \frac{1}{NHW} \sum_{n,h,w} x_{n,c,h,w} \qquad \sigma_c^2 = \frac{1}{NHW} \sum_{n,h,w} \left( x_{n,c,h,w} - \mu_c \right)^2$$ $$\hat x_{n,c,h,w} = \frac{x_{n,c,h,w} - \mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2 + \epsilon}} \qquad y_{n,c,h,w} = \gamma_c \hat x_{n,c,h,w} + \beta_c$$ 因此有 64 个通道时，会得到 64 个均值、64 个方差、64 个 $\gamma$ 和 64 个 $\beta$。BN 不会把 64 个通道混在一起计算一个总均值。 一个小尺寸例子 假设输入是 (N=2, C=3, H=2, W=2)，每个通道参与统计的数字个数是： $$N \times H \times W = 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$$ 三个通道各自用 8 个数计算各自的均值和方差。这个例子也解释了为什么 BN 名字里虽然有 “Batch”，在卷积网络中统计样本数不只是 $N$，还包括 $H \times W$ 个空间位置。 图中每个小方格代表一张 $H \times W$ 特征图。横向是 batch 维 $N$，纵向是通道维 $C$；有颜色的格子表示一起计算均值和方差的范围。 三、公式里每个符号到底是什么 $$\hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \qquad y = \gamma \hat{x} + \beta$$ 符号 来源 是否学习 作用 $x$ 上一层输出 否 待归一化的输入 $\mu$ 当前 batch 或运行统计 否 找到分布中心 $\sigma^2$ 当前 batch 或运行统计 否 衡量分布宽度 $\epsilon$ 人工设定，常为 1e-5 否 防止方差太小导致除零 $\gamma$ BN 参数 是 每通道缩放 $\beta$ BN 参数 是 每通道平移 一个有 $C$ 个通道的 BN 通常有： 可学习参数： $C$ 个 $\gamma$ 加 $C$ 个 $\beta$，合计 $2C$ 个； 状态缓冲量： $C$ 个 running_mean 和 $C$ 个 running_var。 running_mean 和 running_var 会保存到模型文件里，但它们不是通过梯度下降学习的，所以通常不计入 trainable parameters。 四、最关键的知识：训练和推理走两条不同路线 很多 BN bug 都来自没有真正理解这一节。 1. 训练模式：使用当前 mini-batch 当模型处于 model.train() 时： 用当前 batch 的数据计算 $\mu_{\mathrm{batch}}$ 和 $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}$； 用它们归一化当前 batch； 同时更新 running_mean 和 running_var，供以后推理使用。 PyTorch 默认的更新形式可理解为： $$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{running\ mean} &\leftarrow (1 - m)\ \mathrm{running\ mean} + m\ \mu_{\mathrm{batch}} \cr\mathrm{running\ var} &\leftarrow (1 - m)\ \mathrm{running\ var} + m\ \sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}\end{aligned}$$ 其中 $m$ 就是 PyTorch 的 momentum。 PyTorch BatchNorm 默认 momentum=0.1。注意这里的 momentum 写法与一些优化器或其他框架的定义可能相反，阅读代码时要看具体公式。 2. 推理模式：使用训练时积累的运行统计量 当模型处于 model.eval() 时： $$\hat{x} = \frac{x - \mathrm{running\ mean}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{running\ var} + \epsilon}}$$ 当前输入中有哪些其他样本，不再影响统计量。这样同一张图单独预测或与别的图一起预测时，输出应保持一致（忽略数值舍入等因素）。 3. 为什么推理不能继续依赖当前 batch 部署时可能一次只来一张图片，也可能不同请求被任意组合。如果继续用当前 batch： 同一张图片会因为“同批还有谁”而得到不同结果； batch 很小时，均值和方差噪声更大； 线上数据顺序和 batch 组成会意外改变预测。 对 BatchNorm2d 来说，即使 N=1，它通常仍可在 H×W 位置上计算统计量，所以不能简单说输出一定变成常数；真正的问题是这些统计量变成依赖当前单个样本的、与训练运行统计不同的量。 4. model.eval() 不等于“不计算梯度” 这是另一个高频误区： 验证和推理通常两者都要。eval() 本身不会关闭自动求导；no_grad() 也不会自动让 BN 改用运行统计。 五、为什么 BN 往往能让训练更容易 1. 原论文的解释：减少内部协变量偏移 训练时，前面层的参数不断变化，后面层看到的输入分布也随之变化。原论文认为 BN 稳定了中间分布，使后层不必反复追赶。 这个解释很有直觉吸引力，但后续实验表明，即使人为扰乱 BN 后的分布，BN 仍可能加速训练。因此“分布稳定”不能完整解释所有效果。 2. 后续更常见的解释：让优化更平滑 Santurkar 等人在 How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization? 中指出，BN 会让损失和梯度对参数变化更平滑。直观地说： 因此训练通常对初始化更宽容，也常能使用更大的学习率。不过“学习率一定能放大十倍”不是普遍定律，仍需结合网络、优化器和任务验证。 3. BN 带来与 batch 相关的噪声 同一张图片与不同样本组成 batch 时，$\mu_{\mathrm{batch}}$ 和 $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}$ 略有不同，它归一化后的值也会略变。这种随机扰动有时产生类似正则化的效果。 这不等于 BN 可以完全替代 Dropout。二者机制不同，是否同时使用要看任务与实验。 六、小 batch 为什么让 BN 难受 假设要估计全班学生的平均身高： BN 也是如此。batch 较小时： $\mu_{\mathrm{batch}}$ 和 $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}$ 的波动更大； 每次归一化注入更强噪声； 训练时看到的 batch 统计与推理时使用的 running 统计更容易不匹配。 “多小算小”没有脱离任务的固定答案。对普通 2D 分类，单卡每层有较多样本时 BN 常表现很好；对检测、分割和 3D 医学影像，即使 N=1 或 2，显存也可能已经用满，此时往往应认真比较 GroupNorm 或 InstanceNorm。 多 GPU 不等于 BN 看到了全局 batch 普通 nn.BatchNorm2d 在每张 GPU 上独立统计。例如总 batch 为 32、使用 8 张卡时，每张卡可能只用 4 个样本估计统计量。 nn.SyncBatchNorm 会跨进程同步统计量，使 BN 看到更大的有效 batch，但代价是通信开销增加。 梯度累积不能自动增大 BN 的统计 batch 假设每次前向只放 2 个样本，累计 8 次梯度后再更新参数。优化器等效 batch 也许是 16，但 BN 每次仍只用当前 2 个样本计算均值和方差。 这是医学影像训练里非常容易忽略的一点。 七、BN、LN、IN、GN 到底差在哪 它们大多都在做“减均值、除标准差、再缩放平移”，根本差异是：哪些元素被放在一起计算均值和方差。 BatchNorm（BN） 依赖 batch； 训练与推理行为不同； 大 batch 的 CNN 分类中非常常见。 LayerNorm（LN） 对每个样本独立，在指定特征维度上统计。在 Transformer 中通常对每个 token 的隐藏维度归一化；若直接用于 NCHW 图像并归一化 C×H×W，则会把单个样本的通道和空间范围一起考虑。 不依赖 batch； 训练与推理一致； Transformer 和序列模型的标准选择。 InstanceNorm（IN） 每张图单独处理； 会削弱每个实例自己的整体亮度、对比度等“风格”信息； 常用于风格迁移、图像生成，也常见于 3D 医学分割。 GroupNorm（GN） 把通道分成若干组，对每个样本的组内通道和空间位置统计： 不依赖 batch； 小 batch 时通常比 BN 稳定； 检测、分割和显存紧张场景常用。 它们之间还有一个漂亮的关系 对卷积特征使用 GroupNorm 时： 所以 GN 可以看成在 LN 与 IN 之间选择一个分组粒度。注意具体层的可学习参数形状和框架实现仍可能不同，不能只凭这句话机械替换权重。 快速选择表 场景 常见起点 原因 2D 图像分类，单卡 batch 较大 BatchNorm 成熟、高效、预训练模型丰富 目标检测 / 分割，单卡 batch 很小 GroupNorm 不依赖 batch 组成 3D CT/MRI，batch 常为 1–2 InstanceNorm 或 GroupNorm 显存限制下比 BN 稳定 Transformer LayerNorm 对每个 token 独立，不依赖 batch 风格迁移 InstanceNorm 弱化单图对比度与风格统计 这只是可靠的起点，不是不可违反的规则。最终选择应通过验证集和训练稳定性决定。 八、PyTorch 中应该用哪个 BatchNorm 名字里的 1d/2d/3d 主要对应输入的空间维度： num_features 总是通道数 $C$，不是 batch size，也不是图片高宽。 用代码验证训练与推理的差异 查看参数和缓冲量 会看到： 九、BN 与卷积怎么搭配 1. 为什么卷积常写 bias=False 卷积输出可简写为： $$z = \mathrm{Conv}(x) + b$$ 训练时 BN 紧接着减去 batch 均值。对所有空间位置都一样的卷积偏置 $b$ 会同时出现在 $z$ 和 $\mathbb{E}[z]$ 中，减均值时被抵消；之后 BN 自己还有 $\beta$ 负责平移。因此经典的 Conv → BN 结构常写： 2. Conv-BN-ReLU 还是 BN-ReLU-Conv ResNet v1 常用 Conv → BN → ReLU； 预激活 ResNet v2 使用 BN → ReLU → Conv； 不能脱离整个网络结构，只把顺序随意调换并期待预训练权重仍兼容。 3. 部署时可以融合 Conv 与 BN 推理时 running mean/var、$\gamma$、$\beta$ 都是固定的，因此可把 BN 的线性变换折叠进前面的卷积权重和偏置，减少一个运行时算子。许多推理引擎会自动做 Conv-BN fusion。 这只适用于推理态的固定统计，训练时 BN 依赖当前 batch，不能用同样方式永久折叠。 十、冻结预训练骨干时的隐藏陷阱 只关闭梯度： 这会冻结卷积权重、$\gamma$ 和 $\beta$，但不会阻止 BN 在 train 模式下更新 running mean/var，因为运行统计是 buffer，不依赖梯度。 最简单的冻结方式： 但还要注意：之后如果调用整个模型的 model.train()，它会递归地把 backbone 又切回 train 模式。更稳妥的训练代码可以在每个 epoch 开头再次固定骨干，或只把其中的 BN 层切成 eval： 是否同时冻结 $\gamma$、$\beta$ 是另一个选择。eval() 固定的是统计行为，并不会自动把它们的 requires_grad 设为 False。 十一、排查 BN 问题的实用清单 症状 1：训练指标很好，验证指标异常差 依次检查： 验证前是否调用 model.eval()； 验证结束后继续训练时是否恢复 model.train()； 训练 batch 是否太小，running 统计是否可靠； 训练与验证的数据预处理是否一致； 保存和加载时是否遗漏 buffer（正常 state_dict 会包含）。 症状 2：同一张图片单独预测与成批预测结果不同 最先检查模型是不是仍在 train 模式。若已是 eval，再排查随机数据增强、Dropout、非确定性算子和预处理差异。 症状 3：微调后预训练骨干性能崩掉 可能是虽然冻结了参数，BN running 统计仍被小数据集改写。检查各 BN 模块的 .training 属性。 症状 4：batch size 改小后训练明显不稳定 可比较以下方案： 使用 GroupNorm 或 InstanceNorm； 使用 SyncBatchNorm 增大跨卡统计范围； 冻结预训练 BN 的运行统计； 如果任务允许，增大单次前向 batch。 仅靠梯度累积不会让 BN 看到更多样本。 症状 5：模型只有一个数时 BN 报错 训练模式下，每通道可用于计算方差的元素必须足够。例如形状接近 (N=1, C, H=1, W=1) 时，每通道只有一个值，BN 无法得到有意义的 batch 方差，PyTorch 会报错。可增大统计范围、改用其他归一化，或调整结构。 十二、几个容易被忽略的实现细节 eps 是干什么的 如果一个通道里的值几乎完全相同，方差接近 0： $$\frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2}}$$ 可能除以 0 或产生巨大数值。加入一个很小的 $\epsilon$ 保证数值稳定。通常保持框架默认值即可，除非有混合精度或特定数值问题需要调试。 PyTorch 的方差估计细节 PyTorch 文档说明，训练前向中用于归一化的 batch 方差采用有偏估计，而写入 running variance 时使用无偏估计。初学阶段不必手动复现这个细节，但它解释了为什么自己用几行代码手算时，结果可能与框架有轻微差异。 track_running_stats=False 不是普通默认用法 关闭它后，BN 不保存 running mean/var，评估时也会使用当前输入的统计量。这会让结果重新依赖当前 batch。只有明确知道这种行为正是自己所需时才使用。 混合精度下的统计 低精度训练对方差等统计更敏感。成熟的自动混合精度流程通常会为归一化保留合适精度，但自定义算子或手写归一化时要特别小心数值溢出和下溢。 十三、三道自测题 1. 一个 BatchNorm2d 输入为 (8每个通道使用 $N \times H \times W = 8 \times 32 \times 32 = 8192$ 个值。64 个通道分别计算各自的统计量。 2. model.eval() 和 torch.no_grad() 有什么区别？model.eval() 改变 BN 与 Dropout 等层的行为；torch.no_grad() 关闭梯度记录。标准推理通常两者都用。 3. 梯度累积把等效 batch 从 2 变成 16，BN 的统计 batch 也变成 16 吗？不会。BN 在每次前向时就计算统计量，每次仍只看到 2 个样本。梯度累积只推迟优化器更新。 最后用一张清单复习 BN 的核心计算是“减均值、除标准差、再乘 $\gamma$ 加 $\beta$”。 卷积 BN 按通道统计，每个通道跨 $N \times H \times W$ 求均值与方差。 $\gamma$、$\beta$ 是可学习参数；running_mean 与 running_var 是随训练更新并保存的状态。 train 模式使用当前 batch 统计并更新 running 统计；eval 模式读取 running 统计。 model.eval() 与 torch.no_grad() 解决的是两件不同的事。 BN 依赖 batch；batch 太小时，GroupNorm 或 InstanceNorm 往往更稳。 梯度累积不能增大单次前向中的 BN 统计范围。 冻结参数不等于冻结 BN 的 running 统计。 Conv → BN 时，卷积通常使用 bias=False。 参考资料 Ioffe & Szegedy, Batch Normalization, ICML 2015, arXiv:1502.03167 Santurkar et al., How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?, NeurIPS 2018, arXiv:1805.11604 Wu & He, Group Normalization, ECCV 2018, arXiv:1803.08494 Ulyanov et al., Instance Normalization, arXiv:1607.08022 PyTorch, BatchNorm2d 文档
text.en: About 24 minutes · Includes calculations, code and a troubleshooting checklist Batch Normalization is usually shortened to BatchNorm or BN. You will repeatedly see this sequence in network code: It may look like an unimportant standard component, but it affects training speed, learning rate, batch size, validation results and deployment. Almost every convolution in ResNet is followed by BN. If you do not understand how BN differs between training and inference, you can easily encounter problems such as “training is excellent but validation suddenly collapses” or “the same image receives different predictions”. The most intuitive summary is: Within each channel, BatchNorm brings a batch of values back to a more stable numerical scale, then lets the model learn the most useful scale and offset. Before reading: what is normalisation? Imagine two examinations with different difficulty: Looking only at raw scores, 95 appears much better than 70. Once you know each exam’s mean and spread, you can instead ask how far above the corresponding average each score lies. Normalisation does something similar: it considers not only a raw value, but also its position within a distribution. The scale of every neural-network layer changes as parameters are updated. A layer may output mostly within [-1, 1] today and move to [-20, 20] after several optimisation steps. Later layers then face a continuously changing scoring system. BN dynamically standardises these values and helps keep them within a more manageable range. Paper at a glance Paper: Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift Authors: Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy Venue: ICML 2015 Paper: arXiv:1502.03167 The original paper explained BN as reducing “internal covariate shift”. Later work showed that this is not a complete account; smoothing the optimisation landscape and gradients may be more important. This article separates what BN computes, how code behaves and why it may work so that a hypothesis is not mistaken for the definition. 1. Calculate BN by hand with four numbers Temporarily ignore images and channels. Suppose a mini-batch contains only four values: $$x=[\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\ ]$$ Step 1: calculate the mean $$\mu=\frac{1+3+5+7}{4}=4$$ The mean is the centre of this group of values. Step 2: calculate the variance Measure each value’s distance from the mean, square it and average the results: $$(1-4)^2=9 \qquad (3-4)^2=1 \qquad (5-4)^2=1 \qquad (7-4)^2=9$$ $$\sigma^2=\frac{9+1+1+9}{4}=5$$ Variance measures how spread out the values are. Squaring prevents positive and negative deviations from cancelling each other. Step 3: standardise $$\hat{x}=\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}}$$ Ignore the tiny $epsilon$ for the moment. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{5}\approx2.236$: $$\begin{aligned}1 &\longrightarrow (1-4)/2.236 \approx -1.342 \cr3 &\longrightarrow (3-4)/2.236 \approx -0.447 \cr5 &\longrightarrow (5-4)/2.236 \approx +0.447 \cr7 &\longrightarrow (7-4)/2.236 \approx +1.342\end{aligned}$$ The standardised values have a mean close to zero and variance close to one. Step 4: learn a scale and shift BN does not stop at $\hat{x}$. It computes: $$y=\gamma\hat{x}+\beta$$ Suppose the model learns $\gamma=2$ and $\beta=0.5$: $$\begin{aligned}-1.342 &\longrightarrow -2.184 \cr-0.447 &\longrightarrow -0.394 \cr+0.447 &\longrightarrow +1.394 \cr+1.342 &\longrightarrow +3.184\end{aligned}$$ $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are not manually chosen hyperparameters. They are model parameters learned by backpropagation just like convolutional kernels. Why change the values again after standardisation? Forcing every feature permanently to zero mean and unit variance could restrict what the network can represent. $\gamma$ and $\beta$ give it a choice: $\gamma$ stretches or compresses the values; $\beta$ shifts the complete distribution left or right. If the model discovers that the original distribution was useful, it can learn suitable values of $\gamma$ and $\beta$ to restore the required scale and position under the current statistics. BN therefore does not permanently lock all layers to one fixed distribution. 2. Which values does BN average in an image tensor? A convolution normally outputs a four-dimensional tensor: $$(N,\ C,\ H,\ W)$$ Dimension Meaning Example $N$ samples in the batch 8 images $C$ channels 64 feature maps $H$ feature-map height 56 $W$ feature-map width 56 BatchNorm2d(C) computes statistics separately for every channel. For channel c, it collects: That is every spatial position in this channel from every sample: $N\times H\times W$ values. For each channel $c$: $$\mu_c=\frac{1}{NHW}\sum_{n,h,w}x_{n,c,h,w} \qquad \sigma_c^2=\frac{1}{NHW}\sum_{n,h,w}(x_{n,c,h,w}-\mu_c)^2$$ $$\hat x_{n,c,h,w}=\frac{x_{n,c,h,w}-\mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2+\epsilon}} \qquad y_{n,c,h,w}=\gamma_c\hat x_{n,c,h,w}+\beta_c$$ With 64 channels, BN therefore has 64 means, 64 variances, 64 $\gamma$ values and 64 $\beta$ values. It does not mix all 64 channels into one global mean. A small example Suppose the input has shape (N=2, C=3, H=2, W=2). The number of values used for each channel is: $$N\times H\times W=2\times2\times2=8$$ Each of the three channels uses its own eight values to estimate its own mean and variance. This also explains why, despite the word “Batch”, convolutional BN uses not only $N$ samples but also $H\times W$ spatial positions. Each small square represents one $H\times W$ feature map. The horizontal axis is the batch dimension $N$, the vertical axis the channel dimension $C$, and coloured squares are normalised together. 3. What does every symbol in the formula mean? $$\hat{x}=\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}} \qquad y=\gamma\hat{x}+\beta$$ Symbol Source Learned? Purpose $x$ previous layer no input to normalise $\mu$ current batch or running statistics no centre of the distribution $\sigma^2$ current batch or running statistics no width of the distribution $\epsilon$ manually set, often 1e-5 no prevents division by zero when variance is tiny $\gamma$ BN parameter yes per-channel scale $\beta$ BN parameter yes per-channel shift A BN layer with $C$ channels normally has: learnable parameters: $C$ values of $\gamma$ and $C$ values of $\beta$, or $2C$ in total; state buffers: $C$ values in running_mean and $C$ values in running_var. running_mean and running_var are saved in the model file, but they are not learned by gradient descent and are therefore not usually counted as trainable parameters. 4. The most important fact: training and inference take different routes Many BN bugs come from not fully understanding this section. 4.1 Training mode uses the current mini-batch When the model is in model.train() mode, BN: calculates $\mu_{\mathrm{batch}}$ and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}$ from the current batch; uses them to normalise the current batch; updates running_mean and running_var for future inference. PyTorch’s default update can be understood as: $$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{running\ mean}&\leftarrow(1-m)\ \mathrm{running\ mean}+m\ \mu_{\mathrm{batch}} \cr\mathrm{running\ var}&\leftarrow(1-m)\ \mathrm{running\ var}+m\ \sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}\end{aligned}$$ Here $m$ is PyTorch’s momentum, which defaults to 0.1 for BatchNorm. Be careful: some optimisers and frameworks define momentum in the opposite direction, so always check the actual formula. 4.2 Evaluation mode uses accumulated running statistics When the model is in model.eval() mode: $$\hat{x}=\frac{x-\mathrm{running\ mean}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{running\ var}+\epsilon}}$$ Other samples in the current input no longer change the statistics. The same image should therefore produce the same output whether it is predicted alone or alongside other images, apart from numerical round-off and similar effects. 4.3 Why not keep using the current batch during inference? Deployment may receive one image at a time, and requests may be grouped arbitrarily. If inference continued to use the current batch: the prediction for one image would depend on which other images happened to accompany it; very small batches would give noisy mean and variance estimates; the order and grouping of production requests could accidentally change predictions. For BatchNorm2d, even when N=1 it can normally estimate statistics across the $H\times W$ positions, so the output does not necessarily become a constant. The real problem is that these statistics become specific to the current sample and different from the running statistics accumulated during training. 4.4 model.eval() does not mean “disable gradients” This is another common misconception: Validation and inference usually need both. eval() does not disable autograd, and no_grad() does not make BN use its running statistics. 5. Why does BN often make training easier? 5.1 The original explanation: less internal covariate shift As early-layer parameters change during training, the input distribution seen by later layers changes too. The original paper argued that BN stabilises these intermediate distributions, so later layers do not need to keep chasing a moving target. This explanation is intuitive, but later experiments showed that BN can still accelerate training even when the post-BN distribution is deliberately perturbed. Distribution stability therefore does not explain every benefit. 5.2 A common later explanation: smoother optimisation Santurkar et al. argued in How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization? that BN makes losses and gradients respond more smoothly to parameter changes. Intuitively: Training is therefore often more tolerant of initialisation and may support a larger learning rate. “Always multiply the learning rate by ten” is not a universal rule; it still depends on the network, optimiser and task. 5.3 BN introduces batch-dependent noise When the same image appears beside different samples, $\mu_{\mathrm{batch}}$ and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}$ change slightly, so the normalised feature changes slightly too. This random disturbance can sometimes act like regularisation. That does not mean BN completely replaces Dropout. Their mechanisms differ, and whether to use them together depends on the task and experiments. 6. Why are small batches difficult for BN? Imagine estimating a whole class’s mean height: BN faces the same issue. With a small batch: $\mu_{\mathrm{batch}}$ and $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{batch}}$ fluctuate more; every normalisation step injects stronger noise; batch statistics during training are more likely to disagree with running statistics during inference. There is no task-independent threshold for what counts as “small”. BN often works very well in 2D classification when each GPU holds many samples. Detection, segmentation and 3D medical imaging may already exhaust memory at N=1 or 2, in which case GroupNorm and InstanceNorm deserve serious comparison. Multiple GPUs do not automatically give BN the global batch Ordinary nn.BatchNorm2d estimates statistics independently on each GPU. A total batch of 32 across eight GPUs may therefore give each device only four samples for its local estimate. nn.SyncBatchNorm synchronises statistics across processes so that BN sees a larger effective batch, at the cost of extra communication. Gradient accumulation does not enlarge BN’s statistical batch Suppose each forward pass contains two samples and gradients are accumulated for eight passes before the optimiser updates. The effective optimiser batch may be 16, but BN still estimates its mean and variance from only the current two samples each time. This distinction is especially easy to miss in medical-image training. 7. What is the difference between BN, LN, IN and GN? Most of these layers subtract a mean, divide by a standard deviation, then scale and shift. The fundamental difference is: which elements are grouped together to calculate the mean and variance? BatchNorm (BN) depends on the batch; behaves differently during training and inference; common in large-batch CNN classification. LayerNorm (LN) LayerNorm treats every sample independently and normalises over specified feature dimensions. A Transformer normally normalises the hidden dimension of each token. If LN is applied directly to an NCHW image tensor across C×H×W, it includes every channel and spatial position in that one sample. does not depend on the batch; has the same behaviour in training and inference; standard for Transformers and sequence models. InstanceNorm (IN) processes every image independently; suppresses each instance’s global brightness, contrast and other style statistics; common in style transfer and image generation, and also in 3D medical segmentation. GroupNorm (GN) GroupNorm divides channels into groups and calculates statistics over the channels and spatial positions within each group of each sample: does not depend on the batch; is usually more stable than BN with small batches; common in detection, segmentation and memory-constrained training. A useful relationship between them For convolutional features with GroupNorm: GN can therefore be viewed as selecting a grouping scale between LN and IN. Exact learnable-parameter shapes and framework implementations may still differ, so this relationship does not mean pretrained weights can always be swapped mechanically. Quick selection table Scenario Common starting point Reason 2D image classification with a large per-GPU batch BatchNorm mature, efficient, abundant pretrained models Detection or segmentation with a very small per-GPU batch GroupNorm independent of batch composition 3D CT/MRI with batch size 1–2 InstanceNorm or GroupNorm more stable than BN under memory limits Transformer LayerNorm independent for each token and batch-free Style transfer InstanceNorm reduces per-image contrast and style statistics This is a reliable starting point, not an unbreakable rule. Use validation performance and training stability to make the final choice. 8. Which BatchNorm class should you use in PyTorch? The 1d/2d/3d suffix mostly describes the number of spatial dimensions: num_features is always the channel count $C$, not the batch size or image height and width. Verify train/eval behaviour in code Inspect parameters and buffers The output includes: 9. How should BN be combined with convolution? 9.1 Why is convolution often created with bias=False? A convolutional output can be written as: $$z=\mathrm{Conv}(x)+b$$ During training, the following BN subtracts the batch mean. The convolutional bias $b$, which is identical at every spatial position, appears in both $z$ and $\mathbb{E}[z]$ and is cancelled by centring. BN then has its own $\beta$ for shifting. A classic Conv → BN sequence therefore uses: 9.2 Conv-BN-ReLU or BN-ReLU-Conv? ResNet v1 commonly uses Conv → BN → ReLU. Pre-activation ResNet v2 uses BN → ReLU → Conv. The order belongs to the complete architecture. Do not rearrange it casually and expect pretrained weights to remain compatible. 9.3 Conv and BN can be fused for deployment At inference, running mean/variance, $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are fixed. BN’s linear transformation can therefore be folded into the preceding convolutional weights and bias, eliminating one runtime operator. Many inference engines perform Conv-BN fusion automatically. This only applies to fixed inference statistics. During training, BN depends on the current batch and cannot be permanently folded in the same way. 10. A hidden trap when freezing a pretrained backbone Disabling gradients alone: freezes convolutional weights, $\gamma$ and $\beta$, but does not stop running mean and variance from updating while BN remains in training mode. Running statistics are buffers and do not require gradients. The simplest complete freeze is: There is another trap: a later call to the complete model’s model.train() recursively returns the backbone to training mode. Robust training code can restore the frozen state at the start of every epoch, or put only its BN layers into evaluation mode: Whether to freeze $\gamma$ and $\beta$ is a separate choice. eval() fixes the statistical behaviour but does not set their requires_grad flags to False. 11. A practical BN troubleshooting checklist Symptom 1: training metrics are excellent but validation is unexpectedly poor Check in this order: Was model.eval() called before validation? Was model.train() restored before training resumed? Is the training batch too small for reliable running statistics? Are training and validation preprocessing identical? Were buffers lost when saving or loading? A normal state_dict includes them. Symptom 2: one image changes when predicted alone versus in a batch First check whether the model is still in training mode. If it is already in evaluation mode, inspect random augmentation, Dropout, nondeterministic operations and preprocessing differences. Symptom 3: a pretrained backbone collapses after fine-tuning Its parameters may be frozen while small-dataset batches continue to overwrite BN running statistics. Inspect the .training property of every BN module. Symptom 4: training becomes unstable after reducing batch size Compare these options: use GroupNorm or InstanceNorm; use SyncBatchNorm to aggregate statistics across GPUs; freeze running statistics in pretrained BN layers; if the task allows it, increase the batch in each forward pass. Gradient accumulation alone does not let BN see more samples. Symptom 5: BN raises an error when each channel contains only one value Training mode needs enough elements per channel to estimate variance. A shape close to (N=1, C, H=1, W=1) leaves only one value per channel, so PyTorch cannot obtain a meaningful batch variance. Increase the statistical range, choose another normalisation layer or change the architecture. 12. Implementation details that are easy to miss What does eps do? If every value in a channel is almost identical, its variance is close to zero: $$\frac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2}}$$ could divide by zero or produce enormous values. A tiny $\epsilon$ keeps the computation numerically stable. The framework default is normally appropriate unless mixed precision or another specific numerical issue requires debugging. PyTorch’s variance estimates PyTorch documents that the batch variance used to normalise a training forward pass is the biased estimate, while the value stored in running variance uses the unbiased estimate. Beginners do not need to reproduce this detail manually, but it explains small differences between a handwritten calculation and the framework. track_running_stats=False is not the normal default With this option disabled, BN stores no running mean or variance and uses statistics from the current input even during evaluation. Predictions therefore depend on the current batch again. Use it only when that behaviour is deliberately required. Statistics under mixed precision Low-precision training makes variance and similar statistics more sensitive. Mature automatic mixed-precision pipelines normally retain an appropriate precision for normalisation, but custom kernels and handwritten normalisation need special care around overflow and underflow. 13. Three self-check questions 1. A BatchNorm2d input has shape (8Each channel uses $N\times H\times W=8\times32\times32=8192$ values. The 64 channels estimate their statistics independently. 2. What is the difference between model.eval() and torch.no_grad()?model.eval() changes the behaviour of layers such as BN and Dropout. torch.no_grad() disables gradient recording. Standard inference normally uses both. 3. Gradient accumulation changes the effective optimiser batch from 2 to 16. Does BN's statistical batch also become 16?No. BN calculates statistics during each forward pass and still sees only two samples. Gradient accumulation only delays the optimiser update. Final review checklist BN subtracts a mean, divides by a standard deviation, then multiplies by $\gamma$ and adds $\beta$. Convolutional BN calculates statistics per channel across $N\times H\times W$. $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are learned parameters; running_mean and running_var are saved state updated during training. Training mode uses current-batch statistics and updates running statistics; evaluation mode reads the running statistics. model.eval() and torch.no_grad() solve different problems. BN depends on the batch; GroupNorm or InstanceNorm is often more stable when the batch is tiny. Gradient accumulation does not enlarge the statistical range in one BN forward pass. Freezing parameters does not automatically freeze BN running statistics. A convolution immediately followed by BN normally uses bias=False. References Ioffe & Szegedy, Batch Normalization, ICML 2015, arXiv:1502.03167 Santurkar et al., How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?, NeurIPS 2018, arXiv:1805.11604 Wu & He, Group Normalization, ECCV 2018, arXiv:1803.08494 Ulyanov et al., Instance Normalization, arXiv:1607.08022 PyTorch, BatchNorm2d documentation

title.zh: ResNet 残差网络超详细入门：从退化问题到 BasicBlock 与 Bottleneck
title.en: ResNet Explained in Depth: From the Degradation Problem to BasicBlock and Bottleneck

description.zh: 从零理解 ResNet：为什么网络加深后训练误差反而升高，残差 F(x)+x 如何让恒等映射和梯度传播变容易，以及 BasicBlock、Bottleneck、投影捷径与 ResNet-18/50 的结构差异。
description.en: A beginner-friendly guide to ResNet: why training error can rise when a plain network gets deeper, how F(x)+x makes identity mappings and gradient flow easier, and how BasicBlock, Bottleneck and projection shortcuts differ in ResNet-18 and ResNet-50.

text.zh: 阅读约 22 分钟 · 建议边看图边手算 如果只记一句话，可以先记住：ResNet 给信息修了一条“直达电梯”。普通网络要求每一层都重新加工输入；ResNet 允许输入绕过若干层，直接送到后面，再和新学到的变化量相加。 这条看起来只是“一根线”的结构，解决了深层网络很难优化的问题。后来的 DenseNet、SENet、Res2Net 以及大量医学图像分割网络，都在它的思想上继续发展。 阅读前只需要知道三件事 不熟悉下面的词也没关系，先用最朴素的理解即可： 卷积层（Conv）： 用许多小滤镜提取边缘、纹理、形状等特征。 特征图（feature map）： 一层网络处理后的数据。它不一定是能直接看懂的图片，但仍然有高度、宽度和通道数。 反向传播： 模型算错后，把“错了多少”从输出往输入方向传，用它更新每一层的参数。 本文会频繁出现 $N \times C \times H \times W$：$N$ 是一批图片的数量，$C$ 是通道数，$H$ 和 $W$ 是高与宽。 论文名片 论文： Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition 作者： Kaiming He、Xiangyu Zhang、Shaoqing Ren、Jian Sun（MSRA） 会议： CVPR 2016 论文地址： arXiv:1512.03385 核心贡献： 用残差连接稳定训练非常深的卷积网络，并构建了最高 152 层的 ImageNet 模型。 一、为什么当年大家想把网络做深 一张图片进入卷积网络后，浅层通常学习简单特征，深层逐步组合出复杂概念： 直觉上，层数越多，模型能完成的加工步骤越多，应该更容易表达复杂函数。但“能表达”不等于“能训练出来”。在 ResNet 之前，人们发现普通网络加深到一定程度后，效果反而变差。 1. 先区分三个容易混淆的问题 问题 训练集误差 测试集误差 直观解释 过拟合 很低 很高 训练题背得太熟，换题不会 梯度消失 / 爆炸 可能降不动 通常也差 误差信号传不到前层，或数值失控 退化问题 深网比浅网更高 深网也更高 深网理论上更强，却连浅网的解都学不到 ResNet 论文强调的是第三种：退化问题（degradation problem）。 论文在 CIFAR-10 上比较了 20 层和 56 层的普通卷积网络。56 层网络不仅测试误差更高，连训练误差都更高。因此不能把原因简单归结为过拟合。 图中是帮助理解的概念曲线，不是论文实验数据的逐点复刻。重点是看“训练误差”的相对关系。 2. 一个看似简单、实际上很关键的逻辑 假设已经有一个训练好的 20 层网络。现在给它再加 36 层，要得到一个 56 层网络。新加的 36 层什么都不改变，只把输入原样输出，不就至少能保持 20 层网络的效果吗？ “输入什么就输出什么”叫做恒等映射（identity mapping）： $$H(x) = x$$ 从函数表达能力看，56 层网络确实包含这个解。问题是：让几十个“卷积 + 非线性激活”层共同精确拼出 $H(x)=x$，对优化器并不容易。 这就是 ResNet 的出发点：既然深层网络很难自己学会“什么也别做”，那就把“什么也别做”直接写进结构里。 二、残差学习到底在学什么 先把字母解释清楚： 符号 含义 $x$ 残差块的输入 $H(x)$ 希望这个块最终得到的理想输出 $F(x)$ 主分支真正需要学习的“变化量” $y$ 残差块的实际输出 普通网络直接学习： $$y = H(x)$$ ResNet 改成： $$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= H(x) - x \cr y &= F(x) + x \end{aligned}$$ 这里的“残差”就是“目标与输入之间还差多少”。 1. 用修图来理解残差 假设输入 $x$ 是一张曝光稍暗的照片，理想输出 $H(x)$ 是调整好的照片。 普通网络的任务是：从头生成整张调整后的照片。 残差网络的任务是：只生成“哪里提亮多少、哪里增加多少对比度”这张修改清单，然后把修改清单加回原图。 如果原图已经很好： $$H(x) \approx x \quad \Longrightarrow \quad F(x) = H(x) - x \approx 0$$ 模型只要把主分支学到接近 0，就能保留输入。让若干层输出接近 0，通常比让它们共同精确复现 $x$ 容易。 2. 用一个只有数字的例子理解 假设某个特征是 $x = 10$，理想输出是 $H(x) = 10.5$。 普通学习： 直接把 10 变成 10.5。 残差学习： 只学习 $F(x) = 10.5 - 10 = 0.5$，最后 $0.5 + 10 = 10.5$。 如果理想输出正好是 10： 普通学习： 一串层必须共同实现 $H(10) = 10$。 残差学习： 主分支输出 $F(10) = 0$ 即可。 注意，残差不是“预测误差”或“损失值”。它是特征变换前后的差值，在网络内部被主动学习。 三、那条捷径为什么能帮助梯度传播 残差块有两条路： 主分支： 经过卷积、BN、ReLU，得到 $F(x)$； 捷径分支： 输入 $x$ 原样绕过去。 最后把两路按元素相加： $$y = F(x) + x$$ 这里的“相加”要求两边形状完全相同。例如主分支和捷径都必须是 $N \times 64 \times 56 \times 56$。如果形状不同，后面会讲怎么处理。 1. 先理解普通深层网络的梯度 反向传播依赖链式法则。把很多层串在一起时，梯度会不断相乘： $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_0} = g_1 \cdot g_2 \cdots g_n = \prod_{i=1}^{n} g_i$$ 其中 $g_i$ 是第 $i$ 段的局部梯度。 如果每一段大约是 $0.8$，连续乘 20 次： $$0.8^{20} \approx 0.0115$$ 传到前面的信号已经很小。如果每一段都大于 1，又可能越乘越大。这只是直觉示例，真实网络中的梯度是张量而不是单个数字，但问题本质相似。 2. 残差块多出来一个“1” 对 $y = F(x) + x$ 求导，可写成： $$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial F(x)}{\partial x} + 1$$ 因此： $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial F(x)}{\partial x} + 1 \right)$$ 这个 $1$ 来自捷径上的 $x$。即使主分支的局部梯度很小，仍有一部分梯度可以沿着捷径直接向前传播。 更完整地说，跨过多个残差块后，浅层特征不仅通过层层变换传播，还能通过一连串加法路径抵达后层。ResNet 不是让梯度永远不会消失，而是显著改善了深层网络的优化条件。 3. 为什么要“相加”，而不是“拼接” ResNet 使用相加，所以通道数不膨胀，计算量容易控制；而 DenseNet 使用通道拼接，让后层显式看到之前所有层的特征。二者都是捷径，但信息融合方式不同。 四、BasicBlock：ResNet-18 和 ResNet-34 的积木 原始 ResNet v1 的 BasicBlock 主分支包含两个 3×3 卷积： 把顺序背成一句话： 第二个 BN 后面不能先做 ReLU。主分支必须保留正值和负值，再与 $x$ 相加；否则主分支就不能自由地“增加或抵消”输入。 手工跟踪一次形状 假设输入形状是： 两个卷积都是 kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1，所以高宽不变，通道也保持 64： 这里不是把所有数加成一个数，而是对应位置逐个相加： $$y_{n,c,h,w} = F_{n,c,h,w} + x_{n,c,h,w}$$ 其中 $F$ 是主分支的输出 $F(x)$。 五、维度不一样时，捷径怎么办 网络进入新的 stage 时，常做两件事： 高和宽减半，例如 56×56 → 28×28； 通道增加，例如 64 → 128。 此时： 形状不同，不能相加。解决办法是在捷径上放一个 1×1 卷积，并使用 stride=2： 这个 1×1 卷积叫投影捷径（projection shortcut）。它同时完成： 用 stride 2 缩小空间尺寸； 用不同数量的卷积核改变通道数； 让主分支和捷径能够相加。 论文还讨论了补零扩通道等方案。工程里最常见的是：只有尺寸或通道变化时才用 1×1 投影，其他块保留无参数的恒等捷径。 六、Bottleneck：ResNet-50/101/152 为什么不直接堆 3×3 通道很多时，两个 3×3 卷积非常昂贵。Bottleneck（瓶颈块）用三个卷积： 典型例子： “瓶颈”不是说信息一定被严重丢失，而是中间通道数像瓶子中间一样变窄，从而把最贵的 3×3 卷积放在较少的通道上。 1. 为什么 1×1 卷积能改变通道 一个 1×1 卷积核只看同一空间位置，但会同时读取所有输入通道。若输入有 256 个通道，准备 64 个 1×1 卷积核，就能在每个像素位置把 256 维信息混合成 64 维。 它不负责看邻居，主要负责通道混合与升降维。 2. 参数量手算 卷积参数量（忽略偏置）是： $$\text{params} = k_h \times k_w \times C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}$$ 如果始终在 256 通道上做两个 3×3： $$2 \times (3 \times 3 \times 256 \times 256) = 1{,}179{,}648$$ Bottleneck 的主分支： 卷积 参数量计算 参数量 1×1 降维 $1 \times 1 \times 256 \times 64$ 16,384 3×3 处理 $3 \times 3 \times 64 \times 64$ 36,864 1×1 升维 $1 \times 1 \times 64 \times 256$ 16,384 合计 69,632 这个对比是在说明“通道压缩为什么省参数”，不是说两种块的层数完全相同。Bottleneck 有 3 个卷积层，BasicBlock 有 2 个。 3. expansion = 4 是什么意思 标准 Bottleneck 的最后输出通道是中间通道的 4 倍： 所以 PyTorch 实现里会看到 expansion = 4。ResNet-50 最后一个 stage 的输出是 2048 通道，而 ResNet-18 最后是 512 通道。 七、从一个块拼成完整 ResNet 标准 ImageNet ResNet 可以看成： 各型号的差异主要是“用什么块”和“每个 stage 重复几次”： 模型 块类型 四个 stage 的块数 卷积层计数直觉 约参数量 ResNet-18 BasicBlock 2, 2, 2, 2 8×2 + 首层 + FC 11.7 M ResNet-34 BasicBlock 3, 4, 6, 3 16×2 + 首层 + FC 21.8 M ResNet-50 Bottleneck 3, 4, 6, 3 16×3 + 首层 + FC 25.6 M ResNet-101 Bottleneck 3, 4, 23, 3 中间 stage 大幅加深 44.5 M ResNet-152 Bottleneck 3, 8, 36, 3 更深的第三 stage 60.2 M 层数统计通常只数带权重的卷积层和最后全连接层，不数 BN、ReLU、池化和逐元素相加。所以一个 BasicBlock 虽然流程里有很多算子，只贡献 2 个“层数”。 为什么 ResNet-50 和 ResNet-34 的块数相同，名字却不同 两者都是 [3, 4, 6, 3]，合计 16 个块： 八、ResNet v1 与 v2：ReLU 放在哪里很重要 原始 ResNet v1： 后续论文 Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks 提出预激活 ResNet v2： v2 把 BN 和 ReLU 放到卷积前，相加之后不立刻激活。这样多个块串起来时，捷径主干上更接近纯粹的恒等映射，信息和梯度传播更直接。 不要把 v1/v2 与“BasicBlock/Bottleneck”混为一谈： v1/v2 描述算子的排列方式； BasicBlock/Bottleneck 描述主分支的卷积结构。 九、一步步读懂 PyTorch 的 BasicBlock 代码里五个常见疑问 1. 为什么卷积写 bias=False？ 之后的 BatchNorm 自带可学习偏移 beta，卷积偏置会被 BN 的减均值操作抵消，保留它通常是冗余的。 2. 为什么第一个卷积用 stride，第二个固定为 1？ 每个 stage 只需下采样一次。第一层先把尺寸对齐，后续计算都在较小特征图上完成。 3. 为什么是 out + identity，不是拼接？ 残差公式就是逐元素相加，并且相加不会增加通道数。 4. 为什么不推荐 out += identity？ 原地修改可能覆盖自动求导仍需使用的中间值。普通加法更稳妥。 5. nn.Identity() 有什么用？ 它原样返回输入，使代码不必在 forward 里写两套分支。 可以用一段小实验验证形状： 十、初学者最容易犯的七个错误 错误 1：把 residual 当成分类误差 $F(x)=H(x)-x$ 是块内部的特征差值；训练损失则比较最终预测和标签。它们不是一回事。 错误 2：认为捷径完全没有计算 形状不变时捷径是 Identity；形状变化时通常有 1×1 卷积和 BN。 错误 3：把相加写成通道拼接 torch.cat([out, identity], dim=1) 会把通道翻倍，这更像 DenseNet/U-Net 的连接方式，不是标准 ResNet。 错误 4：两路形状不一致就相加 看到 “The size of tensor a must match…” 一类报错，先打印两路的 shape，检查通道、stride 和 padding。 错误 5：把 ResNet 理解为只解决梯度消失 它确实改善梯度传播，但原论文更直接瞄准的是深层普通网络的优化退化。BN、合理初始化等手段已经缓解了朴素的梯度爆炸/消失，残差结构进一步让深网更易优化。 错误 6：认为层数越深一定越适合自己的任务 深网计算更慢、显存更大，也更依赖数据量和训练策略。小数据任务上，预训练 ResNet-18/34 有时比从头训练 ResNet-101 更可靠。 错误 7：忘记输入通道数 ImageNet 预训练模型通常接收 RGB 三通道。灰度医学图像要么复制为三通道，要么改第一层卷积，并考虑预训练权重如何迁移。 十一、在医学图像分割里怎样使用 ResNet U-Net 的编码器本质上负责不断下采样并提取多尺度特征，因此常把普通卷积编码器替换成预训练 ResNet： 这样做有两个常见收益： ImageNet 预训练权重能提供稳定的边缘、纹理等低层特征，对标注稀缺的医学数据很有价值； 残差连接让编码器加深时仍较容易训练。 但要留意输出步长。分类 ResNet 最深特征通常只有输入的 $1/32$，小病灶可能被下采样得过狠。分割模型经常取消后面一次下采样、改用空洞卷积，或依赖强解码器与高分辨率跳跃连接。 十二、从 ResNet 看懂后来的网络 把一个残差块拆成“主分支、捷径、融合方式”三部分，许多后续工作就很好理解： 工作 改了哪里 一句话理解 DenseNet 融合方式 相加改成通道拼接，保留所有旧特征 SENet 主分支出口 相加前为不同通道学习重要性权重 Res2Net 主分支内部 在一个块内制造多尺度层级残差 ResNeXt 主分支内部 用并行分组变换增加“基数” ResNet v2 算子顺序 预激活让恒等捷径更干净 十三、三道自测题 先自己回答，再展开答案。 1. 如果残差块最理想的行为是什么都不改变，主分支应该学到什么？应该学到 $F(x)=0$，这样 $y=F(x)+x=x$。 2. 输入是 64×56×56，主分支输出是 128×28×28，为什么不能直接相加？逐元素相加要求通道、高、宽完全一致。应在捷径上用带 stride=2 的 1×1 卷积，把输入投影成 128×28×28。 3. ResNet-50 为什么用 Bottleneck 而不是 BasicBlock？深层 stage 的通道数很大。Bottleneck 先用 1×1 降通道，让昂贵的 3×3 卷积在窄通道上计算，再升回输出通道，能以可控的参数量和计算量堆得更深。 最后用一张清单复习 ResNet 要解决的是：普通深层网络出现训练退化，不是单纯过拟合。 普通块直接学 $H(x)$；残差块学习 $F(x)=H(x)-x$，输出是 $F(x)+x$。 当理想映射接近恒等时，学习 $F(x)\approx0$ 更容易。 捷径为前向信息和反向梯度提供了直接路径。 BasicBlock 用两个 3×3，服务于 ResNet-18/34。 Bottleneck 用 1×1 → 3×3 → 1×1，服务于 ResNet-50/101/152。 两路形状不一致时，用 1×1 投影捷径对齐。 “残差相加”与 U-Net/DenseNet 的“通道拼接”不是同一件事。 参考资料 He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition, CVPR 2016, arXiv:1512.03385 He et al., Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks, ECCV 2016, arXiv:1603.05027 Xie et al., Aggregated Residual Transformations for Deep Neural Networks, CVPR 2017, arXiv:1611.05431 PyTorch, torchvision.models.resnet 源码
text.en: About 22 minutes · Best read with the diagrams and a few calculations on paper If you remember only one sentence, remember this: ResNet gives information a direct elevator. A plain network asks every layer to process its input again. ResNet lets the input bypass several layers, travel straight to the other side, and then adds it to the newly learned change. That structure looks like “just one extra line”, but it made very deep networks much easier to optimise. Later models such as DenseNet, SENet, Res2Net and many medical-image segmentation networks all develop this idea further. Three things to know before reading It is fine if these terms are new. Start with their simplest meanings: Convolutional layer (Conv): uses many small filters to extract edges, textures, shapes and other features. Feature map: the data produced by a layer. It may not look like an ordinary image, but it still has height, width and channels. Backpropagation: after the model makes an error, it sends information about that error from the output towards the input and uses it to update every layer. This article repeatedly uses $N \times C \times H \times W$: $N$ is the number of images in a batch, $C$ the number of channels, and $H$ and $W$ the height and width. Paper at a glance Paper: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition Authors: Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun (MSRA) Venue: CVPR 2016 Paper: arXiv:1512.03385 Main contribution: residual connections made very deep convolutional networks stable to train and enabled ImageNet models as deep as 152 layers. 1. Why did researchers want deeper networks? When an image enters a convolutional network, early layers usually learn simple features and deeper layers combine them into more complex concepts: More layers provide more processing steps, so a deeper model should be able to represent more complex functions. But being able to represent a function is not the same as being able to learn it. Before ResNet, researchers found that a plain network often became worse after it passed a certain depth. 1.1 Separate three easily confused problems Problem Training error Test error Intuition Overfitting very low high memorises the exercises but fails on new ones Vanishing/exploding gradients may barely decrease usually poor the error signal cannot reach early layers, or its magnitude becomes unstable Degradation a deep network is worse than a shallow one also worse the deep model is more expressive in theory but cannot even learn the shallow model’s solution The ResNet paper focuses on the third problem: the degradation problem. On CIFAR-10, the paper compared 20-layer and 56-layer plain convolutional networks. The 56-layer network had not only a higher test error but also a higher training error. The result therefore cannot be explained simply as overfitting. The curves are conceptual rather than a point-by-point copy of the paper’s experiment. The important part is the relative training error. 1.2 A simple but crucial argument Suppose we already have a trained 20-layer network. We add 36 layers to make it 56 layers. If the 36 new layers change nothing and simply return their input, should the deeper network not at least match the 20-layer one? “Output exactly what you receive” is the identity mapping: $$H(x) = x$$ The 56-layer model contains this solution in terms of representational capacity. The difficulty is optimisation: asking dozens of convolution and nonlinear activation layers to reproduce $H(x)=x$ exactly is surprisingly hard. This is the starting point of ResNet: if a deep stack has trouble learning to do nothing, put “do nothing” directly into the architecture. 2. What does residual learning actually learn? First, define the symbols: Symbol Meaning $x$ input to a residual block $H(x)$ ideal output the block should produce $F(x)$ the change the main branch must learn $y$ actual output of the residual block A plain block learns: $$y = H(x)$$ ResNet rewrites the task as: $$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= H(x) - x \cr y &= F(x) + x \end{aligned}$$ The “residual” is what is still missing between the input and the desired output. 2.1 Think of photo editing Suppose $x$ is a slightly underexposed photograph and $H(x)$ is the corrected photograph. A plain network must generate the entire corrected image. A residual network only needs to generate an edit list describing where to brighten and where to increase contrast, then add that list back to the original image. If the input is already good: $$H(x) \approx x \quad \Longrightarrow \quad F(x) = H(x)-x \approx 0$$ The model can preserve its input simply by making the main branch output nearly zero. That is usually easier than asking several layers to reproduce $x$ exactly. 2.2 A numerical example Suppose a feature has value $x=10$ and its ideal output is $H(x)=10.5$. Plain learning: directly transform 10 into 10.5. Residual learning: learn only $F(x)=10.5-10=0.5$, then compute $0.5+10=10.5$. If the desired output is exactly 10: Plain learning: the complete stack must implement $H(10)=10$. Residual learning: the main branch only needs to output $F(10)=0$. The residual here is not a prediction error or a loss value. It is the difference between input and output features, deliberately learned inside the network. 3. Why does the shortcut help gradients flow? A residual block has two paths: Main branch: convolution, BN and ReLU produce $F(x)$. Shortcut branch: the original $x$ bypasses those operations. The two paths are added element by element: $$y = F(x)+x$$ Addition requires identical shapes. For example, both branches must have shape $N \times 64 \times 56 \times 56$. We will handle mismatched shapes later. 3.1 Gradients in an ordinary deep network Backpropagation follows the chain rule. Across a long sequence of layers, local gradients keep multiplying: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_0}=g_1g_2\cdots g_n=\prod_{i=1}^{n}g_i$$ If every segment is approximately 0.8, then after 20 multiplications: $$0.8^{20}\approx0.0115$$ Only a very small signal reaches early layers. If the factors are repeatedly larger than one, the gradient may instead grow without control. Real gradients are tensors rather than single numbers, but the intuition is the same. 3.2 A residual block contributes an extra “1” Differentiate $y=F(x)+x$: $$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F(x)}{\partial x}+1$$ Therefore: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial F(x)}{\partial x}+1\right)$$ The $1$ comes from the shortcut. Even if the local gradient through the main branch is small, part of the gradient can still travel directly through the shortcut. Across many residual blocks, shallow features reach deeper layers through both transformed paths and a sequence of additive shortcuts. ResNet does not make vanishing gradients mathematically impossible, but it greatly improves the optimisation conditions of deep networks. 3.3 Why addition rather than concatenation? ResNet uses addition, so channel counts do not keep growing and computation stays controlled. DenseNet uses channel concatenation so later layers can explicitly access every earlier feature. Both are shortcuts, but they fuse information differently. 4. BasicBlock: the building block of ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 The main branch of the original ResNet v1 BasicBlock contains two 3×3 convolutions: Memorise the order as one line: There is no ReLU immediately after the second BN. The main branch must retain both positive and negative values before it is added to $x$; otherwise it cannot freely increase or cancel parts of the input. Track the shape by hand Suppose the input is: Both convolutions use kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1, so height, width and channel count remain unchanged: The operation does not sum all entries into one number. It adds matching positions: $$y_{n,c,h,w}=F_{n,c,h,w}+x_{n,c,h,w}$$ Here $F$ denotes the main branch output $F(x)$. 5. What if the dimensions do not match? When a network enters a new stage it commonly does two things: halves height and width, for example 56×56 → 28×28; increases channels, for example 64 → 128. Now the branches have different shapes: They cannot be added. The usual solution is a 1×1 convolution with stride=2 on the shortcut: This is a projection shortcut. It: uses stride 2 to reduce the spatial size; uses a new set of filters to change the number of channels; gives both branches matching shapes so they can be added. The paper also discusses zero-padding the channel dimension. In practice, the common rule is: use a 1×1 projection only when spatial size or channel count changes; otherwise keep the parameter-free identity shortcut. 6. Bottleneck: why ResNet-50/101/152 do not simply stack 3×3 layers Two 3×3 convolutions become expensive when the channel count is large. A Bottleneck uses three convolutions: A typical example is: “Bottleneck” does not mean that useful information must be destroyed. It means the middle channel dimension narrows like the neck of a bottle, allowing the expensive 3×3 convolution to run on fewer channels. 6.1 How can a 1×1 convolution change channels? A 1×1 kernel examines only one spatial position, but it reads every input channel at that position. Given 256 input channels, 64 different 1×1 kernels mix the 256-dimensional vector into 64 output dimensions at every pixel. It does not inspect neighbouring pixels. Its main jobs are channel mixing and dimensionality reduction or expansion. 6.2 Calculate the parameter count Ignoring bias, a convolution has: $$\text{params}=k_hk_wC_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}$$ Two 3×3 convolutions operating entirely at 256 channels require: $$2(3\times3\times256\times256)=1{,}179{,}648$$ The Bottleneck main branch requires: Convolution Calculation Parameters 1×1 reduction $1\times1\times256\times64$ 16,384 3×3 processing $3\times3\times64\times64$ 36,864 1×1 expansion $1\times1\times64\times256$ 16,384 Total 69,632 This comparison demonstrates why channel compression saves parameters; it does not claim the two blocks have the same number of layers. A Bottleneck has three convolutions and a BasicBlock has two. 6.3 What does expansion = 4 mean?
